messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 23
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Environmental Scientist
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 73

She is 23, African, single, and works as an environmental scientist, a role that suits the part of her that likes order, observation, and the quiet reassurance of data. Before the loss, she describes herself as someone who moves easily between fieldwork and planning, comfortable in boots and a safety vest, happiest when she is outdoors measuring water quality or collecting soil samples with a small team. She had been building a life that felt steady enough: work she cared about, close contact with her family, and a brother who, in her telling, was the person she called first for almost everything.

Her brother dies suddenly and unexpectedly, and the event fractures the rhythm of her life. She does not describe the death in a dramatic way so much as in stunned, exact details: the phone call, the strange calm in the voice on the other end, the moment she understands enough to feel the floor drop away beneath her. In the days that follow, she moves through arrangements and condolences almost automatically. She says people around her speak to her in soft voices, as if she might break, and she often feels as though she already has. At the funeral, she stands close to her family and notices everything with an intense, almost unbearable clarity—the smell of flowers, the weight of the heat, the sound of crying that seems to come from somewhere far away and also from inside her own chest.

After the burial, the world does not settle back into place. Instead, it seems to split into a before and after that she cannot bridge. She begins to wake in the night with a sharp, panicked awareness that her brother is gone, followed by a wave of disbelief that can still feel fresh months later. Some mornings she reaches for her phone to text him before remembering. When that happens, she says, it feels like being struck all over again. She starts avoiding his room and the places they used to go together. She cannot look at certain photographs for long. Even ordinary sounds—a ringtone, a knock at the door, a sudden change in someone’s tone—can send her body into immediate alarm. Her heart races, her muscles tighten, and she feels as though she must prepare for something terrible, though she cannot say what exactly.

At work, she continues to function, but with great effort. Her job requires attention, patience, and the ability to track small changes in a landscape over time, and she finds that her mind no longer stays where she puts it. She rereads notes, loses her place in conversations, and catches herself staring at a riverbank or a set of samples without registering what she is seeing. Fieldwork, which once grounded her, now carries a new fragility. Certain sites remind her of family trips, and she finds herself unexpectedly flooded with grief in the middle of routine tasks. She has become more cautious in traffic, more easily startled by sudden movement, and more exhausted by the end of the day than she ever used to be.

She also lives with a constant, punishing loop of thoughts about what she could have done differently. She turns over the final days and hours again and again, searching for a sign she missed, a conversation she should have had, a call she should have made sooner. The questions do not resolve; they deepen. At times she feels guilty for moments of laughter or for being able to keep working at all. At other times she feels angry—at the randomness of the death, at people who say the right things too quickly, at a world that continues moving with such indifference. She does not always know what to do with that anger, so she swallows it, and it settles in her body as tension, headaches, and a constant sense of being on guard.

Her grief is not only sadness but also a persistent sense of unreality. She says that some days she knows, intellectually, that her brother is dead, yet emotionally she still waits for him to come back. That gap between knowing and feeling becomes one of the most painful parts of her experience. She is more isolated now, even when surrounded by family, because she feels she is carrying something that no one else can fully touch. Still, she keeps showing up. She goes to work, answers questions, sends brief replies to friends, and tries to move through each day with the careful endurance of someone navigating unstable ground. In session, she speaks about her brother with tenderness and ache, holding both love and disbelief at once, as if the story of his absence is still too large to fit inside ordinary language.
